source_text: CAPUT TRIGESIMUM, De gubernationis Dei, tribus magnis in res creatas influxibus. Hactenus de gubernatione Dei quantum ad partes et modos: nunc TERTIO agemus de tribus illius magnis influxibus, qui sunt quasi instrumenta unitatis supereminentissimae, quibus vim, sapientiam et amorem suum communicat, et in rebus modificat. II. Sunt autem necessitas, fatum et harmonia. Omnium rerum principium ac gubernatorem, quem Deum nationes appellant, vidimus: nunc de influentiis illius magnis dicendum restat, de necessitate videlicet, fato et harmonia, quae ab illius potentia, sapientia et amore dependent, per quas videmus generationes, mutationes, essentias, operationes et relationes cunctarum rerum absolvi.
english: CHAPTER THIRTY. On the three great influxes of God's governance into created things.

Thus far concerning God's governance as to its parts and modes: now, THIRDLY, we treat of its three great influxes, which are as it were the instruments of a most exalted unity, by which He communicates His power, wisdom, and love, and modifies them in things.

II. They are necessity, fate, and harmony. We have seen the principle and governor of all things, whom the nations call God: it remains to speak of His great influences — namely necessity, fate, and harmony — which depend upon His power, wisdom, and love, and through which we see the generations, mutations, essences, operations, and relations of all things brought to completion.

source_text: Idem in artibus invenimus. Nam architectus graviores amplioresque lapides necessario ponit in fundamento, ne in tecto positi pondere suo deorsum cadant in ruinam domus: leves et ligna in tecto, quia necessitate levia sursum, gravia deorsum tendunt. Hoc vero etiam fato fit ex causarum serie, ut alia sint levia et parva, alia grandia et gravia, et ut suo quoque tempore architectus iis indigat. Et hoc simul resultat in harmoniam, quia gravibus melius est esse infra, et levibus supra, tum gratia sui, tum gratia domus aptius formandae ac firmandae, tum gratia habitatorum. Et quia quod est melius respicit amor, et quod ordinatur respicit sapientia, et quod necesse est esse respicit potestas causarum, ideo influxum potestatis vocamus necessitatem, sapientiae fatum, amoris harmoniam.
english: We find the same in the arts. For the architect necessarily sets the heavier and larger stones in the foundation, lest if placed in the roof they fall downward by their weight into the ruin of the house; the light ones and the timber he sets in the roof, because by necessity light things tend upward and heavy downward.

And this too happens by fate from the series of causes, that some things are light and small, others large and heavy, and that at the fitting time the architect needs them. And this at once results in harmony, because it is better for heavy things to be below and for light above — for their own sake, for the house more aptly formed and strengthened, and for the inhabitants' sake. And because what is better looks to love, what is ordered looks to wisdom, and what must be looks to the power of causes, therefore we call the influx of power necessity, of wisdom fate, of love harmony.

source_text: Exempla sunt obvia in natura et artibus. In natura: pluvia quidem necessitate fit, quia sol vapores sursum necessario elevat, et condensatione accedente hi in pluviam vertuntur, quae gravis facta de necessitate deorsum cadit. Atque id quodam fato fit, concurrente terra vaporabili et solis actione et condensatione e caeli ac temporis dispensatione; ac tandem id resultat in harmoniam, quia tellus per pluviam instauratur et germinat herbas, et nutrit animalia. Idem patet in excrementis. Nam necessario, dum sanguis coquitur, feces combustae remanent; et fato hoc fit ex concursu multarum causarum, panis videlicet manducati, caloris agentis in angusto jecore, et spiritus sequestrantis, quae causae fato convenerunt; idque etiam in harmoniam resultat, et propter melius, quia sanguine mundato feces, ut est melancholia, deserviunt ad excitandum famem in ventriculo, ne pereat animal si non comedat, et ad stimulandum spiritum ad metum malorum et ad contemplationem.
english: Examples are ready to hand in nature and in the arts. In nature: rain comes about by necessity, because the sun necessarily lifts vapors upward, and when condensation is added they are turned into rain, which, grown heavy, falls downward of necessity. And this happens by a certain fate, when vaporable earth, the sun's action, and condensation from the dispensation of heaven and of time concur; and at last it results in harmony, because the earth is renewed by rain, sprouts herbs, and nourishes animals.

The same appears in the excretions. For of necessity, while the blood is cooked, burned feces remain; and this happens by fate from the concurrence of many causes — namely bread eaten, heat acting in the narrow liver, and the spirit that separates — which causes met by fate; and this too results in harmony, and for the better, because when the blood is cleansed the feces (as melancholy) serve to excite hunger in the stomach lest the animal perish if it does not eat, and to stimulate the spirit toward fear of evils and toward contemplation.
